lesson.title: Relief, Recovery, Reform: An Overview of the New Deal
lesson.summary: Roosevelt's New Deal launched an unprecedented wave of federal programs and agencies aimed at providing relief to the suffering, promoting economic recovery, and reforming the financial system to prevent another collapse.
lesson.body:
Historians often summarize the goals of Roosevelt's New Deal using three words: relief, recovery, and reform. Relief meant immediate aid to the unemployed and destitute. Recovery meant restarting economic growth. Reform meant changing the structure of the economy and financial system so that a collapse on the scale of the Great Depression could not happen again. Nearly every New Deal program can be understood as pursuing one or more of these three goals, and many pursued all three at once.

The pace of action in Roosevelt's first hundred days, from March to June 1933, was extraordinary. Within days of taking office, he declared a national bank holiday and pushed the Emergency Banking Act through Congress to stabilize the banking system, a direct response to the wave of bank failures covered in an earlier chapter. The Banking Act of 1933, often called Glass-Steagall, created the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, finally giving ordinary depositors the kind of protection that, had it existed earlier, might have prevented many of the bank runs of the previous years. That same year, the United States effectively moved off the gold standard, a step aimed at fighting deflation and easing the constraints on monetary policy discussed in the chapter on the 1929 crash.

A wave of new agencies followed. The Civilian Conservation Corps put young unemployed men to work on conservation projects. The Agricultural Adjustment Act paid farmers to reduce production in an effort to raise crop prices, directly targeting the overproduction problem described in the chapter on the causes of the Depression. The National Industrial Recovery Act created the National Recovery Administration to set codes for fair competition and wages across industries. The Tennessee Valley Authority built dams and brought electricity and jobs to an impoverished region. The Public Works Administration funded large infrastructure projects, and the Federal Emergency Relief Administration channeled direct relief funding to the states.

Not every program survived legal challenge. The Supreme Court struck down the National Industrial Recovery Act as unconstitutional in 1935 and key parts of the Agricultural Adjustment Act in 1936, forcing Roosevelt's administration to rework its approach. A further burst of legislation around 1935, sometimes called the Second New Deal, added programs such as the Works Progress Administration, which employed millions on public works projects, and the Social Security Act, which created a lasting system of old-age pensions and unemployment insurance.

The New Deal did not, by itself, end the Great Depression. Unemployment remained high through the rest of the 1930s, and full economic recovery would not arrive until the mobilization for World War II. But taken together, these programs eased tremendous suffering, addressed many of the specific weaknesses that had caused the Depression in the first place, from unstable banks to unregulated markets to a lack of any safety net, and permanently reshaped the role the federal government would play in American economic life.
